 Published Nov 15, 2026, 7:00 PM EST 
 Joe Oliveto has over a decade of experience covering tech, physical media, and entertainment. His work has appeared in such digital publications as HuffPost, Thrillist, Yahoo!, Time, Elite Daily, Cracked, and numerous others. Along with collecting physical media, his hobbies include hiking, reading, going to concerts, and attending repertory film screenings throughout NYC.

 If you live virtually anywhere in the U.S., there is a reasonable chance that over the past decade or so, you’ve seen Little Free Libraries crop up throughout communities in your area.
 Add Pocket-lint on Google 
 Add as Preferred Source 
 The Little Free Library is technically a nonprofit organization promoting literacy and access to books. The typical Little Free Library consists of some sort of small container, such as a used newspaper dispenser or a cabinet, where people can both place books for donation and take books out as they please.
 Benefits a Little Free Library offers that don’t necessarily overlap with all the benefits of a traditional library include 24/7 access to books, the ability to install Little Free Libraries in high-need areas where traditional libraries may not be accessible, and breaking down the barriers that might otherwise exclude certain types of books from a local library. For example, in some areas, the people who run the local library may not wish to include certain titles due to ideological reasons or mere personal preference. A Little Free Library ensures they can’t place excessive limits on the types of free books available to readers in a given area.
 If you’re a fan of physical media, particularly DVDs, Blu-rays, and 4K discs, you might wonder if there’s any advantage in setting up a similar type of organization for movies and TV shows.
 Luckily, this already exists. Inspired by Little Free Library, FreeBlockbuster essentially serves the same purpose, but for discs. Obviously named after the most popular video rental chain, it can offer a unique way for both physical media devotees and casual enthusiasts to participate in the physical media resurgence .
 What you need to know about FreeBlockbuster
 The origins of a Little Free Library for physical media
 The idea for FreeBlockbuster began in 2018 when a former Blockbuster employee was thinking of new ways to revamp abandoned LA Times newspaper dispensers in California.
 By late February 2019, they'd established the first Free Blockbuster. Since then, the organization has grown with locations throughout the United States, including on both coasts and through the Midwest, as well as locations in Canada and Mexico.
 It’s also earned attention from both the press and people who work in the industry. For instance, per FreeBockbuster’s website, about a month after the first FreeBlockbuster opened, SE7EN screenwriter Andrew Kevin Walker became the first person ever to return a movie to a FreeBlockbuster. Clearly, it didn’t take long for those who appreciate the appeal of physical media to take advantage of the service.
 How to start a FreeBlockbuster
 You can do your part to spread the word about physical media
 A Free Blockbuster works much the same way a Little Free Library works. Those who wish to start franchises are encouraged to use refurbished newspaper dispensers, but this isn’t a necessity if another container will suffice.
 FreeBlockbuster also offers some limited fully decorated branded boxes. In addition, the organization offers files of their logo, so you can make a stencil to add the FreeBlockbuster brand to your box. Adding the logo in a conspicuous spot may be necessary if you want your box to attract attention, otherwise people may pass it by, not knowing what’s inside.
 Next, all you have to do is fill it up with discs and VHS tapes, as well as other forms of entertainment media you think would appeal to members of your community. You should also contact FreeBlockbuster so they can add your location to their map. Keep in mind, while it would certainly be nice if you could trust that everyone who takes videos and discs from your FreeBlockbuster would also return them in a timely manner, there’s no guarantee this will happen. As such, you should only donate media you don’t mind losing.
 Naturally, you may have to check with local authorities and leaders to determine where you can place a FreeBlockbuster. You may also want to do some community outreach, such as posting on relevant social media platforms and communities, to let people know that your FreeBlockbuster has been set up. If you participate in any local groups with cinephiles as members, you may also want to use this as a platform, as it may be an effective means of getting more donations.
 The potential benefits a FreeBlockbuster offers
 A FreeBlockbuster can get the community excited about physical media again
 A FreeBlockbuster box offers many of the same benefits as a Little Free Library. In an age when physical media is starting to make a comeback, it can also give people a low-cost way to begin experimenting with physical media once again.
 For example, if someone comes across a particularly appealing disc in a Free Blockbuster, it may spark in them the desire to start building a more thorough disc collection. If this happens on a large enough scale, it may generate the type of demand for physical media that paves the way for new video stores in towns throughout the country.
 Of course, that may be a slightly ambitious way of considering FreeBlockbuster’s potential. Nevertheless, if you’ve got some unwanted discs and tapes lying around, they don’t have to keep cluttering your home, nor do they have to wind up in a landfill.
 First, you can check to see if there’s an existing FreeBlockbuster in your area. If so, you can easily make a donation. If not, you may start your own FreeBlockbuster. Along with helping you get rid of some discs and tapes you no longer have use for, it can also provide you with a means of getting your neighbors to re-engage with physical media.
